newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Transrapid head says project still on track.
newsitem.headline: German Transrapid head says project still on track.

text.p: The executive charged with leading private sector involvement in Germany's billion-mark Transrapid magnetic levitation train project on Wednesday dismissed speculation the scheme was commercially unviable.

"I personally am still optimistic that we shall have Transrapid...," Eckhard Rohkamm, head of Thyssen Industrie, the company leading the consortium told a news briefing before a meeting of consortium members.
Earlier on Wednesday the German newspaper Handelsblatt reported that the future of the project, slated to provide a high-speed rail service between Berlin and Hamburg from 2005, was in jeopardy.
Handelsblatt said new projections showed that Transrapid would have to charge much higher fares than previously believed, making it uneconomic. The newspaper did not cite the source of its new data.
The total cost of the project is officially estimated at nine billion marks ($5.5 billion) but critics charge it will inevitably cost a lot more.
Rohkamm said however the commercial viability of the project could not be called into question before the results of a study that are due to be released either in late-March or early April.
"There has as yet been no final appraisal either of the costs of the project or of potential receipts," he said.
Other partners in the project include Siemens AG, and several large German construction companies.

A Transport Ministry spokesman earlier said he had received no indications that private partners planned to pull out of the prestige project. Many questions remain open, and the available facts do not yet warrant a final decision, he said.
Transport Minister Matthias Wissmann has recently said the government stood by its plans to build the controversial Transrapid, but that it would keep a close eye to prevent cost overruns.
The northern state of Schleswig-Holstein, through which the route would pass, has filed suit in the Constitutional Court to block construction, which is due to begin in 1998.
